usage: object 을 — the screen is what you watch
power on with 켜다, not 열다
power off with 끄다, the opposite of 켜다
examples: 저는 텔레비전을 좋아해요.
I like television.
simple: 을 marks the thing you like
저녁을 먹으면서 텔레비전을 봐요.
I watch TV while eating dinner.
everyday: -(으)면서 'while' two actions at once
드라마 보려고 텔레비전을 켰는데 정전이 됐어요.
I turned on the TV to watch a drama but the power went out.
real-situation: -(으)려고 'intending to' + sudden 정전
nuance: 텔레비전 is the full English loanword (television), but in everyday conversation almost everyone shortens it to 티비(TV) — 티비 sounds normal in casual chat while 텔레비전 feels slightly more written or formal. The near-synonym to distinguish is the channel/broadcast itself: 텔레비전 is the physical set or the medium, whereas 방송 means the broadcast/program and 채널 is the channel you flip to. The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb for 'turn on': you must use 켜다 (and 끄다 to turn off), never 열다 'open' — 텔레비전을 열어요 sounds like you are physically prying the box apart. Also remember it is the object of 보다, so it takes 을: 텔레비전을 봐요, not 텔레비전이 봐요.

Saying 텔레비전을 열어요 for turning it on. 열다 means to open a door or lid; an appliance is powered on with 켜다 — say 텔레비전을 켜요.
nuanceMistakeNote: register: 티비 is the spoken default; 텔레비전 leans formal/written.

usage: operate a machine = 돌리다 'spin/run', object 을
고장(이) 나다 'to break down', subject 이
I put it in the washer
I bought a new washing machine
examples: 세탁기가 커요.
The washing machine is big.
simple: 이/가 with a descriptive adjective
빨래가 많아서 세탁기를 돌려요.
I have a lot of laundry so I run the washing machine.
everyday: -아서 reason + 돌리다 for operating it
세탁기를 돌려 놓고 잠깐 나갔다 왔어요.
I set the washing machine running and stepped out for a bit.
real-situation: -아 놓다 'do and leave in that state'
nuance: 세탁기 is Sino-Korean, 洗濯機 literally 'wash(洗)-rinse(濯)-machine(機)', the standard word for a clothes washer. The key collocation an English speaker must memorize is 세탁기를 돌리다 — Koreans 'spin/turn' a washing machine (돌리다) rather than literally 'use' it; the 돌리다 image comes from the drum spinning, and the same verb runs a 청소기(vacuum) or 믹서. Do not say 세탁기를 해요 ('do the washer'), which sounds incomplete, nor 세탁기를 사용해요, which is grammatical but stiff and textbook-ish for daily speech. Distinguish 세탁기 (the appliance) from 빨래 (the laundry / the act of doing laundry) and 세탁 (the formal noun 'laundering', as on a 세탁소 dry-cleaner sign): you 빨래를 하다 'do the laundry' but 세탁기를 돌리다 'run the machine'.

mistakes: Saying 세탁기를 해요 to mean 'run the washer'. 하다 'do' does not collocate here; the fixed verb is 돌리다 — say 세탁기를 돌려요.
Saying 세탁기에서 옷을 넣어요 when loading clothes. 에서 marks where an action happens or a source 'from'; putting something INTO the machine needs the destination 에 — 세탁기에 옷을 넣어요.

usage: instrument 으로 (the tool you clean with)
examples: 청소기가 있어요?
Do you have a vacuum cleaner?
simple: 있다 for possession/existence
주말마다 청소기로 방을 청소해요.
Every weekend I clean my room with the vacuum.
everyday: 마다 'every' + instrument 으로
밤늦게 청소기를 돌리면 아랫집에서 시끄러워해요.
If I run the vacuum late at night, the downstairs neighbor finds it noisy.
real-situation: -(으)면 condition + apartment etiquette
nuance: 청소기 is Sino-Korean, 淸掃機 'clean(淸)-sweep(掃)-machine(機)', and is itself the everyday short form of 진공청소기 (眞空, 'vacuum-cleaning machine'); in normal speech nobody says the full 진공청소기. Two particles compete and English speakers mix them up: use 으로 when the vacuum is the TOOL you clean with (청소기로 청소해요 'clean WITH the vacuum'), but 을 when the vacuum is the OBJECT you operate (청소기를 돌려요 'run the vacuum'). Like the washing machine, you 돌리다 'run/spin' it, not 하다. Distinguish the appliance 청소기 from the activity 청소 'cleaning' (청소를 하다 'do the cleaning') — the 기(機) suffix is precisely what turns the activity-noun into the machine that performs it, the same 기 in 세탁기 and 선풍기.

Saying 청소기를 해요. As with other appliances the verb is 돌리다 'run', so say 청소기를 돌려요; 하다 alone doesn't work.

usage: power on with 켜다, object 을
power off with 끄다, the opposite of 켜다
colloquial 틀다 'put on' (very common for AC)
examples: 방에 에어컨이 있어요.
There is an air conditioner in the room.
simple: 있다 for existence + place 에
너무 더워서 에어컨을 켰어요.
It was so hot that I turned on the AC.
everyday: 너무 'too' + -아서 reason, past tense
에어컨을 켜 놓고 자면 감기에 걸릴 수 있어요.
If you sleep with the AC left on, you can catch a cold.
real-situation: -아 놓다 'leave on' + -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 'might'
nuance: 에어컨 is a clipped English loanword (air con(ditioner)) — Korean kept only the first half, which is why it looks shorter than the English source. For switching it on you have two natural verbs: 켜다 'turn on' (general, pairs with 끄다 'turn off') and the very colloquial 틀다 'put on/start running', which Koreans love for the AC, fan and radio (에어컨 좀 틀어 줘 'put the AC on for me'). The English-speaker pitfall is 열다 'open': 에어컨을 열어요 is wrong because you are not opening a door — power-driven machines are 켜다/끄다 or 틀다. Note 에어컨 is the cooling appliance; the heating equivalent is 난방 (or a 히터), and central building climate control is 냉난방, so do not stretch 에어컨 to mean 'heater'.

nuanceMistakeNote: loanword (clipped 'air con'); 켜다/틀다 to start, 끄다 to stop.

usage: power on with 켜다, object 을
colloquial 틀다, very common for fans
I sit in front of the fan
examples: 여름에는 선풍기를 켜요.
In summer I turn on the fan.
simple: 에는 topic-time + 켜다
더울 때 선풍기 바람을 쐬면 시원해요.
When it's hot, it feels cool to catch the fan's breeze.
everyday: -(으)ㄹ 때 'when' + 바람을 쐬다 'catch a breeze'
에어컨이 없어서 선풍기로 버텨요.
I don't have an AC so I get by with a fan.
real-situation: -아서 reason + 으로 means + 버티다 'hold out'
nuance: 선풍기 is Sino-Korean, 扇風機 'fan(扇)-wind(風)-machine(機)' — literally a machine that makes fan-wind — so the 기(機) ending matches 세탁기/청소기. The contrast learners need is with 부채, the hand-held folding fan you wave manually: 선풍기 is the electric standing/desk fan you plug in, 부채 is the non-electric one. Switch it on with 켜다 or the colloquial 틀다 (선풍기 틀어 줘 'put the fan on'); never 열다. A characteristic collocation is 선풍기 바람 'the fan's breeze' and 바람을 쐬다/쏘이다 'to catch the wind'. Culturally you may hear about 선풍기 괴담 ('fan death', the urban myth that sleeping with a fan on can kill you) — useful to recognize even though it's just folklore.

nuanceMistakeNote: 한자: 扇風機 fan-wind-machine; electric 선풍기 vs hand 부채.

usage: I put it in the fridge
I take it out of the fridge
문 'door' + 열다 (open the door, not 'power on')
examples: 부엌에 냉장고가 있어요.
There is a refrigerator in the kitchen.
simple: 에 place + 있다
우유를 냉장고에 넣어 두세요.
Please put the milk in the fridge (and keep it there).
everyday: -아 두다 'put and keep', polite request
냉장고에 먹을 게 하나도 없어서 배달시켰어요.
There was nothing to eat in the fridge so I ordered delivery.
real-situation: 먹을 게 'something to eat' + 하나도 없다 'none at all'
nuance: 냉장고 is Sino-Korean, 冷藏庫 'cold(冷)-store(藏)-warehouse(庫)', i.e. a storehouse that keeps things cold. The contrast English speakers must internalize is the IN/OUT particle pair: putting food IN uses the destination 에 (냉장고에 넣다), taking it OUT uses the source 에서 (냉장고에서 꺼내다) — many learners over-use 에서 for both. Note that unlike a TV you DO open the fridge with 열다 because you literally open its door (냉장고를 열다 / 냉장고 문을 열다); but you never 'turn it on' day to day. Distinguish the whole appliance 냉장고 (the fridge, chilled section) from the 냉동고/냉동실 'freezer (compartment)', built on 冷凍 'freeze' rather than 冷藏 'cold-store'; 김치냉장고 is the dedicated kimchi fridge found in most Korean homes.

Calling the freezer 냉장고. The chilled section is 냉장고/냉장실, but the freezer compartment is 냉동실 (冷凍 'freeze') — keep them separate.
nuanceMistakeNote: 한자: 冷藏庫 cold-store-house; into 에 (넣다) vs out of 에서 (꺼내다).

usage: I heat it in the microwave
instrument 으로 (heat WITH it) + 데우다 'warm up'
I put it in the microwave
colloquial 돌리다 'run' even of the microwave
examples: 전자레인지가 있어요?
Is there a microwave?
simple: 있다 existence question
식은 밥을 전자레인지로 데워 먹어요.
I warm up cold rice in the microwave and eat it.
everyday: 식다 'go cold' modifier + 으로 means + 데워 먹다
전자레인지에 금속 그릇을 넣으면 불꽃이 튀어요.
If you put a metal bowl in the microwave, sparks fly.
real-situation: -(으)면 condition + safety warning
nuance: 전자레인지 is a hybrid word: Sino-Korean 電子 'electronic' + the English loan 'range' (oven/cooktop), so literally 'electronic range' — Koreans rarely say the full thing and shorten it to 레인지 in casual talk. The natural cooking verb is 데우다 'to warm up' (전자레인지로 음식을 데우다), and colloquially people even say 전자레인지에 돌리다 'spin it in the microwave', borrowing the 돌리다 'run' image from washers and vacuums. The particle pitfall mirrors the vacuum: 으로 when the microwave is the TOOL you heat WITH (전자레인지로 데워요), 에 when it is the place you put food INTO (전자레인지에 넣어요). Don't confuse 데우다 'reheat/warm' with 끓이다 'boil' or 굽다 'grill/bake' — a microwave 데우다s, it doesn't 끓이다.

Saying 전자레인지로 밥을 끓여요 for reheating rice. 끓이다 is 'boil'; warming food in a microwave is 데우다 — say 밥을 데워요.

usage: static location 에 with 앉다 (the spot you end up sitting)
dynamic action 에서 (where the resting happens)
I lie down on the sofa
examples: 거실에 소파가 있어요.
There is a sofa in the living room.
simple: 에 place + 있다
소파에 앉아서 텔레비전을 봐요.
I sit on the sofa and watch TV.
everyday: -아서 'sit and then' sequential + the sitting spot 에
소파에 누워서 자다가 목이 아팠어요.
I fell asleep lying on the sofa and my neck hurt.
real-situation: -다가 'while doing, then switched' + result
nuance: 소파 is the English loanword 'sofa', the Western-style upholstered couch for a living room; the everyday native alternative for a long bench-seat is rarely used, so 소파 is the default word. The sharp grammar point is 에 vs 에서 with this noun: use 에 for the END-POINT of a positioning verb — 소파에 앉다 'sit (down) on the sofa', 소파에 눕다 'lie on the sofa' — but 에서 when an ongoing ACTIVITY happens there — 소파에서 쉬다/책을 읽다 'rest / read on the sofa'. English 'on the sofa' hides this split, so learners wrongly say 소파에서 앉아요. A common collocation is 편한 소파 'a comfy sofa'; a sofa-bed is a 소파베드.

Using 에 for an activity done on the sofa: 소파에 쉬어요 should be 소파에서 쉬어요, because resting is an ongoing action and its setting takes 에서.
nuanceMistakeNote: loanword; 앉다/눕다 take 에 (end-point), 쉬다/읽다 take 에서 (activity).

usage: I put it in the wardrobe
I hang it in the wardrobe
I take it out of the wardrobe
examples: 방에 옷장이 있어요.
There is a wardrobe in the room.
simple: 에 place + 있다
겨울 코트를 옷장에 걸어 둬요.
I hang the winter coat in the wardrobe (and leave it).
everyday: 걸다 'hang' + -아 두다 'keep in that state'
옷장이 꽉 차서 옷을 정리해야 해요.
The wardrobe is packed full so I need to sort my clothes.
real-situation: 꽉 차다 'be packed' + -아야 하다 'have to'
nuance: 옷장 combines native 옷 'clothes' + the bound morpheme -장 (from the hanja 欌, 'wooden cabinet/closet'), so it is a clothes-cabinet — the same -장 appears in 책장 'bookshelf' and 찬장 'cupboard'. The near-synonyms to separate: 옷장 is the freestanding wardrobe/closet for clothes; 서랍장 is a chest of drawers; 붙박이장 is a built-in closet; and the small bedside one is a 협탁. Verbs split by how the clothes sit: 넣다 'put in' for folded items, 걸다 'hang' for things on hangers, and 꺼내다 'take out'. The particle pitfall is the same IN/OUT contrast as the fridge: into the wardrobe is 에 (옷장에 넣다), out of it is 에서 (옷장에서 꺼내다).

usage: object 을 + 열다 (you do open a drawer)
object 을 + 닫다, opposite of 열다
I put it in the drawer
examples: 서랍에 양말이 있어요.
There are socks in the drawer.
simple: 에 location + 있다
서랍을 열어서 가위를 꺼냈어요.
I opened the drawer and took out scissors.
everyday: -아서 'open and then' sequential + 꺼내다
서랍이 안 열려요. 뭔가 걸린 것 같아요.
The drawer won't open. Something seems to be stuck.
real-situation: 안 열리다 'won't open' (passive) + 걸리다 'be caught'
nuance: 서랍 is a native Korean word (no hanja) for a single sliding drawer; a piece of furniture made of several stacked drawers is a 서랍장 'chest of drawers'. Unlike powered appliances, a drawer is genuinely opened and closed, so it correctly takes 열다 'open' / 닫다 'close' — the contrast to notice is 열다 (you actively open it) versus the passive 열리다 'be/get opened' used when it won't budge (서랍이 안 열려요 'the drawer won't open'). As the object you act on, 서랍 takes 을/를 (서랍을 열다), but as a destination it takes 에 (서랍에 넣다). A handy collocation is 맨 위 서랍 'the top drawer' / 맨 아래 서랍 'the bottom drawer'.

usage: fixed verb 치다 'draw across', object 을
examples: 창문에 커튼이 있어요.
There is a curtain on the window.
simple: 에 place + 있다
햇빛이 너무 세서 커튼을 쳤어요.
The sunlight was too strong so I drew the curtains.
everyday: 세다 'be strong' + -아서 reason, past
자기 전에 커튼을 치고 불을 꺼요.
Before sleeping I draw the curtains and turn off the light.
real-situation: -기 전에 'before' + 고 listing two actions
nuance: 커튼 is the English loanword 'curtain', the fabric window cover. The verb pitfall is severe: to close/draw curtains across a window the fixed verb is 치다 (커튼을 치다 'draw the curtains'), and to open them you 걷다 'gather aside' (커튼을 걷다) — note 치다 here means 'spread/draw across', the same 치다 as in 텐트를 치다 'pitch a tent', NOT 치다 'hit'. Do not say 커튼을 해요 'do the curtain', which is incomplete, and be careful that 열다/닫다 'open/close' sound less idiomatic than 걷다/치다 for curtains specifically. Distinguish 커튼 (cloth, on a window/stage) from 블라인드 'blinds' (the slatted kind): a thick light-blocking curtain is an 암막 커튼.

usage: I shelve it on the bookshelf
꽂다 'insert upright' (slot a book in), destination 에
I pull it off the shelf
examples: 방에 책장이 있어요.
There is a bookshelf in the room.
simple: 에 place + 있다
다 읽은 책을 책장에 꽂아요.
I shelve the books I've finished on the bookcase.
everyday: 다 읽다 'finish reading' modifier + 꽂다
책장에 책이 너무 많아서 한 줄 더 쌓았어요.
There were too many books on the shelf so I stacked another row.
real-situation: -아서 reason + 쌓다 'pile up'
nuance: 책장 combines 책 (冊 'book') + -장 (欌 'cabinet/case'), literally a book-cabinet, the same -장 as in 옷장 'wardrobe'. Watch a tricky homograph: 책장 also means 'a page/leaf of a book' (책장을 넘기다 'turn the page'), so context decides between 'bookshelf' and 'page'. The signature verb is 꽂다 'to slot/stand upright' for putting a book in (책을 책장에 꽂다) and 빼다/꺼내다 to take it out — 꽂다 captures sliding the spine into the row, far more natural than 넣다 here. Near-synonym: many people also say 책꽂이 (책+꽂이, from 꽂다) for a bookshelf, often a smaller open rack, whereas 책장 tends to be the larger cabinet-style unit. Into the shelf is 에, off the shelf is 에서.
